Introduction
Rotator cuff tendinopathy refers to pain and weakness, generally experienced with
movements of shoulder external rotation and elevation, because of excessive load on
rotator cuff tissue.1
Definitions
Classifications/spectrum of tissue disorder
Intrinsic factors, including overload may cause tendon dysfunction.
Extrinsic factors play a role in tendon dysfunction.
Tendon compression is a less likely mechanism of some tendon disorders.
Tendinopathy: degeneration of the tendon without visual evidence of tearing
Partial-thickness tear: tearing that disrupts only the articular surface or the bursal surface of
the tendon
Full-thickness tear: tearing with evidence of continuous tendon disruption between the
articular and bursal sides

Definitions
Rotator cuff disorders comprise the classification or spectrum of tissue disorders of the
rotator cuff tendons, ranging from tendinopathy, to partial-thickness rotator cuff tears,
to full-thickness rotator cuff tears. Tendon disorders of the rotator cuff may be
mechanistically related to intrinsic and extrinsic factors, leading to tendon degeneration
over time. Sudden overload also may lead to an acute tear, which may be an acute-on-
chronic tear.
Intrinsically, rotator cuff tendon disorders may be caused by tensile/shear overload and
by alterations in biology, vascularity, and mechanical tendon properties. Extrinsically,
tendon compression within the subacromial space was commonly considered a primary
factor for tendon disorders; however, current evidence indicates compression is a less
likely mechanism of tendon disorders in patients with some forms of tendinopathy.

Tendinopathy can be defined as tendon degeneration without visual evidence of tearing.
Characteristic signs are microtearing and changes in macromorphology (thickening
initially), micromorphology (eg, neovascularity and alterations in collagen organization),
and mechanical properties. Commonly, tendinopathy also may be referred to as
subacromial pain syndrome because specifically identifying the tendon as the source of
symptoms and excluding the bursae or other structures in the subacromial space may
be difficult. Another name, subacromial impingement syndrome, is less favorable,
because the mechanism of tendon impingement in the subacromial space is recognized
as a less likely cause of tendon disorder.2
A partial-thickness tear can be defined as a tear of the rotator cuff tendon through
degenerative or acute mechanisms, which only partially disrupts the tendon from the
articular and bursal sides.3,4 A full-thickness tear can be defined as any tear within the
rotator cuff tendon, via degenerative or acute mechanisms, that produces a continuous
tendon disruption between the articular and bursal sides of the tendon regardless of
size.3,4

In determining the proper plan of care, surgical management typically is considered;
however clinical decision making involves consideration of factors beyond the presence
of tendon pathology or injury. The size, type, and location of the tear are important tear
characteristics to determine. The quality of the tissue and healing potential must be
assessed. Several patient-specific factors, including comorbidities, prior and current level
of function, and functional goals, must be considered during clinical decision making.
Psychological factors and social determinants of health also are important to consider in
developing a surgical treatment plan. The Optimal Screening for Prediction of Referral
and Outcome is a short screening tool that consists of questions from 11 scales that can
affect outcomes.5 Social determinants of health that can affect overall outcomes may
include socioeconomic status, race, ethnicity, family support, and language
understanding. Modifiable risk factors associated with poorer outcomes include higher
body mass index, comorbidities, diabetes mellitus, smoking, preoperative stiffness, and
affected mental and behavioral health. Nonmodifiable risk factors include patient age,
worker’s compensation claims, and the already mentioned social determinants of
health.6
Basic Concepts of Rehabilitation
Rehabilitation is critical to successful outcomes in patients who undergo treatment for rotator
cuff disorders.
Preoperative and postoperative rehabilitation are warranted.
Rehabilitation may be similar for tendinopathy, partial-thickness tears, and full-thickness tears.
Postoperative rehabilitation is contingent on postoperative conditions. 

Basic Concepts of Rehabilitation
The role of rehabilitation in the management of rotator cuff disorders is to assist in
attaining optimal outcomes, including pain control, enhanced mobility and range of
motion (ROM), improved motor control and strength capacity of the rotator cuff and
periscapular musculature, and the highest level of function possible. Preoperative and
postoperative rehabilitation are critical for patients with a rotator cuff disorder.
Preoperatively, rehabilitation may be similar for patients with tendinopathy, patients

will exist between patients based on their level of irritability and function. Postoperative
rehabilitation is variable and must be appropriate for the surgical procedures
performed. In addition, factors included in surgical decision making also must be
considered in designing a formal rehabilitation program.
Differences in Rehabilitation Interventions
Frequency and duration
Dosing
Progression
Protection versus loading versus overloading


Differences in Rehabilitation Interventions
Differences in rehabilitation interventions and the overall rehabilitation plan exist
between patients and between diagnoses. The frequency and/or the duration of an
episode of care depends on the stage or phase of recovery. Early stages of rehabilitation
may focus on symptom control and self-management strategies, whereas later stages of
rehabilitation may focus on mobility, strength, and function. Dosing of specific
rehabilitation interventions, including exercise prescription, manual physical therapy,
and modalities, may vary based on patient tolerance and response. Graded progression
through the course of interventions and through the overall episode of care also varies
based on patient tolerance, response, and the stage of tissue healing. In working
through a rehabilitation program, the rehabilitation provider must constantly balance
protection of recovering tissue against appropriate tissue loading against overloading to
increase capacity. Careful consideration is required to balance the need of mobility
versus stability, specifically for shoulder rehabilitation.

Pathoanatomic model of diagnostic categories alone may not effectively guide treatment

Patient-specific factors, including tissue irritability and impairments, must be considered to

Pathoanatomic diagnosis in combination with patient-specific factors of tissue irritability and
identified impairments will guide intensity/dosage of the rehabilitation plan. 

Staged Approach for Rehabilitation
Because of the multifaceted nature of rotator cuff disorders, the pathoanatomic model
of diagnostic categories alone may not effectively guide decision making for
rehabilitation for patients undergoing surgical or nonsurgical treatment. Patient-specific
factors must be considered to effectively guide rehabilitation. Tissue irritability should be
assessed and can be categorized as low, moderate, or high. Assessment of tissue
irritability should delineate the severity and/or intensity of symptoms, the time to onset
after aggravating factors, the time to return to baseline after alleviating factors, and the
duration symptoms. Physical impairments should be identified during physical
examination. Impairments may include deficits in motor control, muscle weakness,
decreased muscle capacity, flexibility limitations, or mobility restrictions. Pathoanatomic
diagnoses in combination with the patient-specific factors of tissue irritability and
identified impairments will guide the intensity and dosage of the rehabilitation plan
based on the physical stress theory. The overall approach for rehabilitation should be
staged.7 Table 1 lists common shoulder impairments associated with progressively
intense intervention tactics across a spectrum of tissue irritability.7

Surgical Management Versus Nonsurgical Rehabilitation
Patient education on medical diagnosis, disease progression, and possible outcomes are
paramount to allow patients to decide the best course of action.8
Exercise approach should be the first treatment option; however, patient goals, values, and
shared decision making must be considered.9
The most important predictor of failed nonsurgical management is patient expectations.
Patients with a full-thickness rotator cuff tear report improvement in pain and functional
outcome scores with nonsurgical treatment or surgical repair; however, patients who are
offered and elect to undergo rotator cuff repair report greater improvement in outcome
scores and reduced pain compared with patients who elect to undergo nonsurgical treatment.
Better outcomes are independently associated with younger age, shorter symptom duration,
and rotator cuff repair.10


In considering surgical management versus nonsurgical rehabilitation, patient education
on medical diagnosis, disease progression, and possible outcomes are paramount to
allow patients to decide the best course of action.8 Nonsurgical rehabilitation based on

pathoanatomic conditions, the most important predictor of failed nonsurgical
management is patient expectations. Patients with a full-thickness rotator cuff tear who
undergo nonsurgical treatment or surgical repair report improved pain and functional
outcome scores; however, patients who are offered and elect to undergo rotator cuff
repair report greater improvement in outcome scores and reduced pain compared with
patients who elect to undergo nonsurgical treatment. Better outcomes are
independently associated with younger age, shorter symptom duration, and rotator cuff
repair.10
American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons Recommendations
Strong evidence supports patient-reported outcomes improve with physical therapy; however,
in patients with deleterious tissue characteristics, tears may progress with nonsurgical
treatment.

Moderate evidence supports that healed rotator cuff repairs result in improved patient-
reported functional outcomes compared with physical therapy and unhealed rotator cuff

For small- to medium-sized rotator cuff tears, strong evidence supports that physical
therapy and surgical management result in considerable improvement in patient-
reported outcomes, specifically for patients with a symptomatic small to medium full-
thickness rotator cuff tear. In considering the long-term nonsurgical management of
symptomatic small to medium full-thickness rotator cuff tears, strong evidence supports
improved patient-reported outcomes with physical therapy; however, rotator cuff tear
size, muscle atrophy, and fatty infiltration may progress with nonsurgical management.

Prognostic Surgical Decision Making
Surgical treatment should be considered in patients who do not improve after an exercise
regimen.11,12
Arthroscopic surgery and supervised exercise are better treatment options than a placebo11,12
Limited evidence shows that surgical management is not more effective for symptomatic
rotator cuff tears than nonsurgical management.13
In comparing subacromial decompression surgery, arthroscopic surgery alone, and
nonsurgical management, the surgical treatment groups had improved outcomes for shoulder
pain and function compared with the nonsurgical treatment group14
Differences in objective and subjective outcomes exist in patients who undergo surgical
treatment for a full-thickness rotator cuff tear15
No clinically meaningful difference exists between surgical management and physiotherapy
versus physiotherapy alone at 3-month, 6-month, 1-year, 2-year, and 5-year follow-up.9
No clinically meaningful difference exists between surgical management and physical therapy
versus placebo surgical management and physical therapy with regard to clinical outcomes of
pain and function at 3-month, 6-month, 1-year, and 2-year follow-up.9
Strong evidence supports conversion to full-thickness or transtendinous/in situ repair in
patients with a high-grade partial-thickness rotator cuff tear in whom nonsurgical treatment
fails.4
Moderate evidence does not support acromioplasty as a concomitant treatment option
compared with arthroscopic repair alone in patients with a small to medium full-thickness
rotator cuff tear.4
Moderate evidence supports distal clavicular resection in combination with arthroscopic repair
in patients with a full-thickness rotator cuff tear and a symptomatic acromioclavicular joint.4
In young and active patients, rotator cuff tendon repair for small to medium tears
demonstrates little benefits in the first years postoperatively, with improvements in outcomes
over time.16
Older age is associated with higher failure rates and poorer patient-reported outcomes after
rotator cuff repair.4

Prognostic Surgical Decision Making
Surgical treatment should be considered in patients who do not improve after an
exercise regimen.11,12 Arthroscopic surgery and supervised exercise are better
treatment options than a placebo; however, the difference between the two active
treatment options is not considerable.11,12 In comparing surgical management and
nonsurgical management via physical therapy, limited evidence shows that surgical
management of symptomatic rotator cuff tears is not more effective than nonsurgical
management.13 Multiple factors, such as tear characteristics and prognostic patient
factors, must be considered.
In comparing subacromial decompression surgery, arthroscopic surgery alone, and
nonsurgical management, surgical management results in improved outcomes for
shoulder pain and function compared with nonsurgical management; however, a
clinically important difference has not been demonstrated.14 In comparing objective and
subjective outcomes, a statistically significant difference has been reported in patients
with a full-thickness rotator cuff tear who undergo surgical treatment; however, the
difference is not clinically important.15

between surgical management and physical therapy compared with physical therapy
alone at 3-month, 6-month, 1-year, 2-year, and 5-year follow-up.9 In addition, no

Prognostic Nonsurgical Rehabilitation Decision Making
In considering nonsurgical rehabilitation for the management of rotator cuff tears,
prognostic indicators must be examined during clinical decision making. In comparing
arthroscopic surgery with nonsurgical rehabilitation, strong evidence demonstrates no
substantial difference in long-term patient-reported outcomes (>1 year) with regard to
healing rates; however, arthroscopic surgery is associated with better short-term
improvements in postoperative recovery of motion and decreased visual analog scale
scores.4 In examining tissue characteristics, non-repaired small to moderate rotator cuff
tears demonstrated moderate anatomic deterioration, muscle atrophy, and fatty
degeneration during 8.8-year follow-up; however, satisfactory or better outcomes have
been reported.17 In a study of patients with a full-thickness rotator cuff tear (>5-year
follow-up), Boorman et al19 reported that 75% of the patients were successfully treated
nonsurgically. The patients in whom nonsurgical treatment failed and who subsequently
underwent surgical treatment achieved similar quality of life scores at 5-year follow-up
compared with the patients who did not undergo surgical treatment.
Ultrasonographic-guided needling, radial extracorporeal shockwave therapy, and high-
energy focused extracorporeal shockwave therapy are adjunctive treatment options that
may help alleviate pain and achieve complete resolution of calcium deposition, with
high-energy focused extracorporeal shockwave being substantially superior in achieving
functional recovery compared with ultrasonographic-guided needling and radial

Rotator Cuff Rehabilitation
Pain Generators
Pain generators may be associated with the affected rotator cuff tendon tissue or may lie
outside the rotator cuff in the adjacent shoulder structures.
Physical therapy may aid in identifying potential pain-generating tissue and developing an
individualized plan of care to address the specific source of pain and contributing pain factors.
The plan of care and management should be individualized based on the pain generator and
the pathologic tissue.
Patients’ experience of pain often is multifactorial and beyond the pathoanatomic diagnosis,
and a holistic approach will be required to mitigate pain-generating factors and the pain
experience/perception (consider top-down generator of pain).

Pain Generators
In patients with rotator cuff disorders, pain generators may be associated with the
affected rotator cuff tendon tissue or may be in the adjacent shoulder structures (ie,
bursae, long head of the biceps, posterior glenohumeral capsule, anteroinferior
glenohumeral ligament, etc.). Physical therapy may aid in identifying potential pain-
generating tissue. In addition, physical therapy may aid in developing an individualized
treatment plan to address the specific source of pain and contributing pain factors in
relation to nonsurgical, preoperative, and postoperative management. The treatment
plan should be individualized based on the pain generator and the pathologic tissue,
with a goal to return patients to their prior level of function. Patients’ experience of pain
often is multifactorial and beyond the pathoanatomic diagnosis. A holistic approach is

Range of Motion
Includes passive range of motion (PROM), active-assisted range of motion (AAROM), and active
range of motion (AROM)

Range of Motion
ROM is the process by which a joint moves through its available range. In patients with a
rotator cuff disorder, ROM may be limited at the glenohumeral joint, the
acromioclavicular joint, the sternoclavicular joint, and the scapulothoracic joint. PROM is
the process by which an extrinsic outside force moves a joint through its ROM in
absence of intrinsic muscle contraction. AAROM is the process by which a combination
of extrinsic force and intrinsic muscle force moves a joint through its ROM, often against
gravity. This often describes the initial stages of muscle contraction with external
assistance. AROM is the process by which an intrinsic muscle force moves a joint through
its ROM, often against gravity, without external assistance. This often describes the
subsequent stages of muscle contraction, commonly described as strengthening.
Typically, ROM involves moving through a joint’s available range; however, treatment
options may be focused on improving quality and quantity of ROM. One such treatment
option is joint mobilization. Joint mobilization is the application of external forces to a
joint, by an individual or equipment, to improve pain or tissue extensibility of the joint
capsule and/or the surrounding tissues. Improved joint mobility may lead to improved
ROM.

Stretching
Stretching is the process by which restricted and shortened muscles are lengthened to
improve soft-tissue mobility, thereby improving ROM. Stretching should not be confused
with ROM. Passive stretching is the process by which a muscle is being lengthened with
no activity from the muscles of the joint involved. Active stretching is the process by
which patients use their antagonist muscle to stretch, causing a reciprocal inhibition of
the agonist muscle and often may help with pain and muscle tone.20
Strengthening
Strengthening is the process of applying a resistive load to induce muscular contraction to
stimulate adaptation to respond to the load.
Strengthening of the rotator cuff muscles and the periscapular muscles most likely will result
in diminished pain and improved stability and control.

Strengthening
Strengthening is the process of applying a resistive load to induce muscular contraction
to stimulate adaptation to respond to the load, which improves muscle strength,
endurance, and/or hypertrophy. Strengthening of the rotator cuff muscles and the
periscapular muscles most likely will result in diminished pain and improved stability and
control.20

Motor Control
Motor control refers to centrally mediated and peripherally controlled movement.
Motor-control exercises are exercises and activities aimed to promote neuromuscular
control of muscle contraction and neuromotor recruitment patterns/activity/timing.
Measured and controlled movement requires coordination of muscular activation and
control of body limb segments and joints. This incorporates proprioceptive feedback,
neurologic feedback, and intrinsic muscle and joint responses to generate accurate and
appropriate movements.20
Muscle Contractions
Includes isometric, concentric, and eccentric contractions

Muscle Contractions
Muscle contractions include isometric, concentric, and eccentric contractions. These
contractions create different stresses, forces, and movements across a joint. Isometric
muscle contractions are muscle contractions with no appreciable change in muscle
length or joint motion during force production. Concentric muscle contractions are
muscle contractions that shorten muscle fibers during force production, causing the
origin and insertion of the muscle to move toward each other, with associated changes
in joint ROM. Eccentric muscle contractions are muscle contractions that lengthen
muscle fibers during force production, causing the origin and insertion of the muscle to
move away from each other, with associated changes in joint ROM.
Muscle Exercise Types
Includes isometric exercises, isotonic exercises, and isokinetic exercises

Muscle Exercise Types
Isometric exercises involve muscle contractions against a resistance without a change in
joint position; these exercises are commonly used early in the rehabilitation process to
provide strengthening and limit atrophy in patients with mobility or ROM restrictions.
Isotonic exercises involve muscle contractions resulting in changes throughout ROM
against a load, typically against gravity. the load may be constant; however, the torque
applied to the joint will vary depending on the level arm of the joint. Isokinetic exercises
involve muscle contractions through a fixed speed and varying resistance based on the
force exerted through the ROM; isokinetic testing commonly is performed with the use
of an isokinetic dynamometer machine to assess if full muscle strength has been
regained.
Closed Versus Open Kinetic Chain Exercises
Closed kinetic chain exercises are exercises in which the distal extremity is in contact with a
solid and stable object. 
Open kinetic chain exercises are exercises in which the distal extremity is not in contact with a
solid and stable object, such as a table or wall. 

Closed Versus Open Kinetic Chain Exercises
Closed kinetic chain exercises are exercises in which the distal extremity (ie, hand and
foot) is in contact with a solid and stable object (eg, floor, table, wall). These exercises are
performed in the early stages of rehabilitation because they provide greater joint
stability. Typically, closed kinetic chain exercises safely stimulate co-contraction of the

Rehabilitation Before Rotator Cuff Surgery
Patients with a rotator cuff tear have risk factors detrimental to the recovery process.
Rehabilitation or a physical therapy plan that is initiated before rotator cuff surgery helps
optimize preoperative status. Optimizing and addressing any risk factors or deleterious
confounding factors preoperatively maximizes postoperative outcomes. Physical therapy

nonsurgical rehabilitation and are based on the staged approach for rehabilitation.7 The
goals of preoperative rehabilitation include minimizing pain, maximizing mobility,
restoring normal ROM, optimizing strength, enhancing motor control, educating patients
on postoperative precautions/restrictions, managing outcome expectations regarding
surgical management and rehabilitation, and assessing patient acceptable symptom
state.

Communication between the patient, the surgeon, and the physical therapist is vital to
guide the rehabilitation process. The surgeon and the physical therapist must maintain
continuity of care, including sharing of information relevant to the initial surgical
findings, the surgical procedures, the initial postoperative precautions and restrictions,
and rehabilitation progression. Rehabilitation after rotator cuff repair is a long process. If
rehabilitation is on target with the timeline, milestones, and pain and functional
improvements, referral back to the surgeon is not necessary.
Scenarios in which a patient should be referred back to a surgeon should include the
following: the patient has pain that is limiting progress, and remediation of pain via a
trial of different modalities fails; the patient is not improving despite
compliance/adherence and patient education; the patient does not achieve milestones
for ROM goals postoperatively; the patient has recalcitrant stiffness or limited
improvements in ROM after 4 to 6 weeks; the patient is progressing well and suddenly
